page.title: Septic arthritis
about: Symptoms of septic arthritis include sudden severe pain, redness and swelling in a joint, and may include high temperature.

lines.text: The main symptoms of septic arthritis are:
sudden severe pain in a joint
not being able to move or put weight on the affected joint
hot, swollen or red skin over the affected joint – redness may be harder to see on black or brown skin
a high temperature (fever) – although not everyone has one.
Symptoms of septic arthritis usually develop quickly over a few days and need to be checked straight away.

cards.headline: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:

lines.text: you have severe joint pain, usually in just 1 joint, that started suddenly
you have swelling around a joint
the skin around a joint has changed colour
you find it difficult to move a joint
you have pain in a joint and feel generally unwell and have a high temperature, or feel hot, cold or shivery
If you cannot get an urgent GP appointment, call 111 or get help from 111 online .
If you have septic arthritis you’ll usually be admitted to hospital for treatment. This may include:
antibiotics given straight into a vein
a procedure to drain fluid from the affected joint
antibiotic tablets to take for several weeks after you leave hospital
The average stay in hospital if you have septic arthritis is about 2 weeks. Most people start feeling better quickly once they are given antibiotics.
Important

If you're given antibiotic tablets when you leave hospital, it's important to keep taking them for as long as you are told to, even if you feel better. Stopping treatment too soon could lead to the infection coming back.
Follow-up treatment
You may be referred to a physiotherapist to help you get the joint moving again. This should help prevent any long-term stiffness in the joint.

If the infection is in an artificial joint, such as in a knee or hip replacement, the joint may need to be removed. It may be possible to replace it with a new artificial joint once the infection has been treated.
You can get septic arthritis if germs get into a joint. This can happen:
if you have an injury or accident affecting a joint
if germs from somewhere else in the body spread into the blood and then into a joint
as a complication of joint surgery
Anyone can get septic arthritis but some people are more at risk. This includes people:
with rheumatoid arthritis
with a weakened immune system
who have recently had joint surgery
who have an artificial joint, such as a knee or hip replacement
who inject drugs like heroin
who have diabetes
with gonorrhoea, which is a sexually transmitted infection
